customize.text:
No one knows about the parents of the hero Nare Magan Sundjatta and what tribe they came from, but his lineage has never been tainted by ancient royalty. Story and song say Sundjatta was born over five hundred years ago, blessed by the stars of dawn. At that time, the ruler of the Children of Echoes tribe was Mbande, the mother of mines and gems. She chose young Sundjatta as the tribe's hero and miner, even though the iron hammer was then larger than the boy himself. Despite this, the boy wielded the hammer as though he were the wind itself, chiseling into the great mountain, sparks flying from its handle.
When Mbande returned to the Night Kingdom, Sundjatta was already a young man, robust beyond his years. On the night when the people were choosing a new leader, Sundjatta left the tribe. He was the strongest in the tribe, but power did not appeal to him. Instead, he sought to find a proud testament to his existence in the Children of Echoes. Filled with determination, Sundjatta set out on a journey through unknown lands, but from then on, the tribe regarded him as a traitor. Sundjatta, who had lost his good name, headed to the distant lava lake, letting the scorching waves burn his body. At that time, the lake was home to the evil dragon Lukwata, who dreamed of restoring dragon rule. When the war between humans and dragons destroyed its tribe, it hid in a dark mountain cave. The dragon's eyes were blinded by sulfuric fumes, its mind was clouded, and Lukwata was unaware that Natlan had come under human rule fifteen hundred years earlier. And when Sundjatta invaded its lair, he saw that the legendary dragon had long since grown decrepit and lost its mind. Sundjatta laughed, swung his hammer, and said mockingly to the dragon:

<color=#ffffffd9>"I am merely a nameless miner, not some contemptible knave."</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"Just as you are no king — merely a tottering lizard!"</color>

Although the dragon was old, its rage was terrifying. The heat of the magma scorched Sundjatta's hair and eyebrows, and the dragon's fierce venom again seeped into flesh and viscera, the unbearable agony burning deep. Its massive, yellowed fangs left festering wounds, while sharpened claws tore open old scars, but the young man continued to swing his hammer. Only when the dragon's rock-hard skull cracked and Lukwata perished did Sundjatta lie down — truly now did he deserve a hero's name!

When Sundjatta returned to the tribe, he was finally elected as the chief of the Children of Echoes and head of the mines. Once, before the Cataclysm, the Nanatzkayan miners worked day and night for months to make an important item. This item was essential to the safety of the mines and the tribe's survival, and the elders named it the "Mountain-Bracing Bolt." Whenever the earth began to shake and the mountains began to move, peace could only be purchased by way of tribute, thrown to the mountain spirits in their deepest caverns. Young Sundjatta mocked this ritual and decided to discover the cause of the collapses. He followed the rocky arteries and, in the deepest caverns, discovered the gate into spaces deeper still. This was the forbidden land of the tyrant Och-Kan, where no human had set foot for a thousand years, but the chief found marks of recent excavations. Tunnels wound underground like snakes, and no one knew where they led. Eventually, Sundjatta followed an underground river and saw a faint glimmer flickering at the exit of the tunnel. There, he saw the ruins of the bastion belonging to the usurper of Cinder City and the refuge of ancient miners. When Och-Kan aimed to erase the traces of draconic craft, the ancestors of the Children of Echoes fled through these tunnels into the deserted mountains. This secret passage was discovered by a blind Stegosaurus that resided within the rocky cliffs. And although the secret passage was sealed, bloodthirsty monsters still managed to sneak through. To defend their home atop Tequemecan Valley, the tribe's warriors armed themselves with sharp blades and long spears and fought fiercely against the monsters in the dark caves. And so the battle raged for days and nights without number, until the nightmarish howling and the sounds of clashing stone and metal stopped as one. This was the Mountain-Bracing Bolt. It bestowed a blessing upon those who had once remained hidden and who fought for their freedom and their land, only to fall before daybreak, those who sacrificed themselves so that dawn might come. This blessing still endures to this very day.

During his reign, Sundjatta approached the Pyro Archon with a request to support the exile of a warrior named Tenoch, due to his love of battle. But when a black wave swept across Natlan, it was Tenoch who took up his obsidian club and set out to unite the disputing tribes. Before Sundjatta, Tenoch had already been joined by four heroes from different tribes, and Sundjatta, along with his Stegosaurus companion, Muhuru, became the fifth. Realizing that this battle could be Natlan's last, the chief of the mines set out to fight, asking that the Children of Echoes not be drawn into it. A total of six heroes from six tribes followed Tenoch. All of them bore the same Ancient Names as the six heroes accompanying the first Pyro Archon, Xbalanque. Sundjatta bore the Ancient Name

During the war with the Abyss, the Natlanese calculations estimated that they would have a maximum of five hundred years before the Night Kingdom was completely lost to the Abyss, but at that time, Natlan lay in ruins, and the civilization was dying. It was necessary to unite the tribes, otherwise, it would be impossible to dream of a final victory. So, the Archon had a long and involved discussion with the heroes of each tribe, and finally came up with a five-hundred-year-long plan to save Natlan. During this time, the Archons and chiefs were to rebuild the tribes, and when the time came, the Wayob would again choose six heroes of Natlan with the Ancient Names of Xbalanque's companions.

The chief of the mines had known Mavuika since her childhood, from the moment she asked to be trained, declaring she would become the future Pyro Archon. At first, Sundjatta was reluctant to take her, but she claimed she would shoot those cornflakes in his kitchen from dozens of meters away. And when the girl actually did shoot the cornflakes, the Children of Echoes’ chief agreed to train her. Years later, Mavuika proposed a plan to save Natlan, and Sundjatta trusted her. He was among those who went to the final battle alongside the heroes of Natlan and Mavuika, after which she imbued her life in the Sacred Flame, to be reborn five hundred years later and carry out her plan. During this battle, Sundjatta rushed to rescue the hero of the Collective of Plenty, taking the blow himself, but in the end, everyone died anyway. Only the Pyro Archon was able to reach the Sacred Flame, thanks to a warrior from the People of the Springs who died before her throne. When the time came for the Pyro Archon's plan to be carried out, Sundjatta's spirit helped the heir of his Ancient Name, Xilonen, give Mavuika power to fight the Abyss.

desc.text:
O craftsman who unrolls these scrolls, my name is Nare Magan Sundjatta, the 52nd chief of Nanatzcayan. I am Mbande's successor. I shall be like Daurama, Nayoga, and Sanhaj. I will weave ancient texts into a tapestry, I shall speak of the foundations of phlogiston-forging, and spare you needless detours.
…
Chapter V: Another Possibility for Phlogiston-Forging Techniques
According to the scroll left behind by our great-mother, Sakkuk, the techniques of phlogiston-forging originated from the ancient dragons. In their era, there existed a more marvelous forging method beyond present imagination, one that directly forged Phlogiston into different materials.
Such mastery was witnessed by Sakkuk, and the founding pioneer, Ixquieh, earned her title as "Hero of the Forged Flame" by truly understanding how to smelt phlogiston itself. She was no dragon — but having had no parents to grant her a name, she named herself in draconic tongue and style. So in theory, mastery of this advanced phlogiston-forging art was within human reach.
Regrettably, Ixquieh's manuscripts number few and far between. She set fire to her own workshop, including her writings about forging, and took her own life while forcing her brother do the same, to avoid his leaving a tarnished legacy like that of Och-Kan. In a sense, it was she who slew her own kin, Teteocan's first chief. I cannot pass judgment on that choice, as each era has its morals. Yet the loss of such craftsmanship is regretful, and haunts future smiths still.
The 13th chief, Hun Toh, — may fire bless his name — spent his entire life trying to grasp the art of phlogiston-forging, but found no success. I tried it in my youth and failed as well. To you, smiths of future ages: You may try, but do not squander your years and strength. For weaving matter with phlogiston is like building an unshakable house from ground Grainfruit dust, all while tracking the placement of each speck. One misstep, and the entire structure will collapse. Based on my experience, with our current technological constraints, ordinary humans cannot attain this great endeavor. Therefore, I advise you to focus on using phlogiston as a supplementary material for tempering metals and jade rather than treating it as the foundational substrate of your forging.
But this does not spell our defeat, nor our inability to surpass our ancestors and the ancient dragons. Remember, phlogiston is but a tool, and as a craftsman, it is your hand that guides the tool, not the other way around. After all, only a craftsman — you, a human — can materialize ideas and concepts into reality.
In fact, many recorded ideas from Sakkuk's time have been realized by now, even though no smith in these centuries has ever mastered the forging of phlogiston itself. Take, for instance, golden discs that preserve song and melody, platforms suspended briefly aloft by phlogiston, or vehicles that may carry us over all manner of terrain. Such marvels abound! Future generations of craftsmen — may they live in peaceful times — might build upon these techniques to achieve wonders beyond our era's imagination. This is the legacy of Nanatzcayan: A "blessing" born of mortal hands, not the boon of gods or masters.
